images.filename: Stele of Khoiniki District with mosaic.jpg
images.caption: An abandoned roadside stele "Khoiniki District" located within the Polesie State Radioecological Reserve (PSRER). The site is part of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. The mosaic featuring a wheat ear, a gear, and Belarusian folk ornaments has remained preserved in its original state since the 1986 disaster. The former highway is currently closed to public traffic.

The former highway is currently closed to public traffic.

images.caption: The Babchin checkpoint (KPP Babchin) in the Khoiky District, Gomel Region, Belarus. This is the main entry point to the Belarusian part of the Chernobyl exclusion zone (PSRER). The photo shows a blue and yellow gate with a sign saying "STOP! SHOW YOUR PERMIT", a guard building with a red roof and a local dog.
images.alt: The Babchin checkpoint (KPP Babchin) in the Khoiky District, Gomel Region, Belarus. This is the main entry point to the Belarusian part of the Chernobyl exclusion zone (PSRER). images.caption: A yellow-and-red triangular radiation hazard sign with an additional plate reading "Attention! Area with a high level of plutonium contamination", standing among bare spring trees. The sign marks a part of the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve contaminated by the 1986 Chernobyl disaster. Taken on 20 April 2026 near the former village of Krasnoselye, Khoiniki District.
images.alt: A yellow-and-red triangular radiation hazard sign with an additional plate reading "Attention! Area with a high level of plutonium contamination", standing among bare spring trees. The sign marks a part of the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve contaminated by the 1986 Chernobyl disaster. Taken on 20 April 2026 near the former village of Krasnoselye, Khoiniki District.

images.filename: Krasnoselye PSRER Dirt road with firebreak 2026-04-20.jpg
images.caption: An unpaved forest road with a newly ploughed mineral firebreak strip running parallel to it. Such firebreaks are routinely maintained in the Polesie Reserve to prevent wildfires on radioactively contaminated lands. A small painted memorial stone marking the former settlement is visible at the right edge of the road.
images.alt: An unpaved forest road with a newly ploughed mineral firebreak strip running parallel to it. Such firebreaks are routinely maintained in the Polesie Reserve to prevent wildfires on radioactively contaminated lands. A small painted memorial stone marking the former settlement is visible at the right edge of the road.

images.caption: A boulder painted red with a white panel bearing the handwritten inscription "Krasnoselye. 244 inhabitants. Resettled in 1986". The marker stands at the site of the village evacuated after the Chernobyl disaster and is part of the educational route inside the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve.

images.caption: A rural cemetery in a pine forest with blue and dark metal crosses, ornate cast-iron grave fences and artificial flowers. The cemetery belongs to the former village of Krasnoselye (Khoiniki District), evacuated in 1986 after the Chernobyl disaster, and now lies inside the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve.

images.caption: A long rusted metal fence with a fallen lattice section; behind it are rows of blue metal crosses and grave enclosures among pine trees. The cemetery belongs to Krasnoselye, a village evacuated after the Chernobyl disaster, and is located inside the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve.

images.caption: A tall red-and-black steel fire watch tower with an observation cabin on top, antenna and a solar panel, standing on a sandy rise. Such towers are used for early detection of forest fires in the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve, the Belarusian part of the Chernobyl exclusion zone.

images.filename: Krasnoselye PSRER Aerial view of abandoned village 2026-04-22.jpg
images.caption: A wide aerial view of a former settlement: scattered wooden houses and outbuildings with slate roofs among overgrown gardens, meadows and young trees. The village was evacuated after the Chernobyl disaster and is now part of the Polesie State Radiation-Ecological Reserve in Khoiniki District.
